findings.problem: Approach 2 is labelled 'copy on write' in four places (the approach tag from 5.4 s, the 'copy on write' tag over the 4,600 x 75 = 345,000 sum, caption 6 'Copy on write: 345,000 a second.', and the 'most users: copy on write' card). The lesson (ds-twitter, 'Approach 2: fan out when you write', the Approach 2 segment button 'fan-out on write', takeaways 'fan-out') and the lecture call it FAN-OUT ON WRITE. 'Copy-on-write' is a different, well-known OS/storage technique, so a learner who knows it is misled, and the lecture's key term 'fan-out' never appears on screen at all (only in the file name).
findings.fix: Rename every 'copy on write' to 'fan-out on write' (approach tag 'Approach 2: fan-out on write', the sum tag, the hybrid card 'most users: fan-out on write', caption 'Fan-out on write: 345,000 a second.'). Keep the plain-words caption 'Approach 2: copy to each follower.' (it describes it correctly) and show the word 'fan-out' once next to the five outgoing copies (a small tag 'fan-out: 1 post, 5 copies').
findings.evidence: ds-1 s8@6.4 ('Approach 2: copy on write'), s8@12.8 (tag + caption), s8@15.9 (hybrid card); lesson js/content/ds/ds-05.js L['ds-twitter'] and js/content/ds/ds-03.js segment 'Approach 2: fan-out on write'.

findings.problem: 'A celebrity needs 87 seconds: go hybrid.' and the red '87 s' bar are not in the lesson. The lesson says 30 million writes for one tweet is too slow against a 5 s goal and the scale card gives the real figure: it would need 6,000,000 writes/s (30,000,000 / 5 s) against the 345,000/s the whole system does. The video invents 30,000,000 / 345,000 = 87 s by assuming one celebrity tweet gets the system's entire average write rate (which is already used by the 4,600 other posts a second). The arithmetic is right (86.96) but the premise is the author's, stated as fact in the caption. The caption also starts at 13.6 s, but the '87 s' label only appears at about 14.4 s (bar still empty at 14.2 s).
findings.fix: Use the lesson's framing: bar 1 '30,000,000 copies', goal '5 s', result tag '6,000,000 writes/s needed (17 x the 345,000 we have)'. Caption e.g. 'A celebrity needs 6,000,000 writes a second: go hybrid.' If the 87 s idea is kept, label it 'at 345,000 a second it would take 87 s' and start the caption when the number is on screen (about 14.4 s). In the storyboard json change 'celeb.secs 87' accordingly and drop the D1.TWEET.celeb.secs assertion or add celeb.needPerSec = 6,000,000.
findings.evidence: ds-1 s8@14.2 (caption says 87 seconds, bar has no number yet), s8@15.9; lesson ds-03.js sdraw(): 'so that would need 6M writes/s for just this one tweet'; D1.TWEET.celeb = {followers 30000000, target 5, secs 87}.

findings.problem: The lesson's central claim is never stated: Twitter chose approach 2 BECAUSE reads outnumber posts (ds-twitter step 'Why Twitter chose approach 2', predict ds-tw-1). The video shows '65 reads per post' (caption 5) and then jumps to '345,000 a second' (caption 6) with no sentence linking them, so the opening question 'Do the work on write or on read?' gets no explicit answer except the final hybrid card; a first-time learner can read 345,000 as a downside of approach 2 and not understand why it still wins.
findings.fix: Make caption 5 'Reads outnumber posts 65 to 1: so work on write.' (or add a short tag 'so: do the work once, when posting') and caption 6 'Fan-out on write: 345,000 writes a second, but reads become one lookup.'
findings.evidence: ds-1 s8@9.9 and s8@12.8 (captions 5 and 6); lesson ds-05.js step 'Why Twitter chose approach 2'.

findings.problem: The costs £34,297 / £8,800 / £44,000 and 'none above 32x' are shown as plain facts. In the lesson they come from an 'Illustrative cost model' (vertical = 1000 x c^1.7, no machine bigger than 32x, commodity machines = 1000 each plus about 10% overhead) and the lesson never says these are real prices. Nothing on screen says 'example'; the odd-looking £34,297 reads like a measured price and the learner cannot tell where it comes from.
findings.fix: Add a small grey tag under the banner, e.g. 'example prices' (or 'made-up cost model'), and/or show the basis once ('1x = £1,000'). Keep the numbers (verified: 1000 x 8^1.7 = 34,297; 1.1 x 8 x 1000 = 8,800; 1.1 x 40 x 1000 = 44,000; 7/8 = 87.5% shown as 88%).
findings.evidence: ds-1 s9@3.6 (£34,297 vs £8,800 with no qualifier); lesson ds-04.js text 'Illustrative cost model: ...'.

findings.problem: The scene presents scale out as simply better and ends on 'just add more' (green). The lesson frames this as TRADE-OFF 2 and states the price of scaling out: machines must coordinate, stay consistent and handle partial failures (and one machine is simpler at small sizes). Scene 3 is labelled 'TRADE-OFF 1' but this scene's kicker is 'SCALABILITY', so there is no 'trade-off 2' and no downside shown for the winning option.
findings.fix: Change the kicker to 'TRADE-OFF 2' and add one orange tag on the scale-out column, e.g. 'but: machines must coordinate' (shown after 'capacity left 88%' or with 'just add more'), or caption 4: 'At 40 times, only scale out works, but it must coordinate.'
findings.evidence: ds-1 s9@10.6 ('just add more', no downside); lesson ds-05.js step 'Costs scale better, but it's harder to coordinate' and ds-why 'Trade-off 2: one big machine vs many cheap ones'.

findings.problem: While the data-access layer is on screen and before the change is replayed (about 8.5 s to 10.0 s), the 'to edit' counter still reads a grey '5', left over from the no-layer case. Next to 'connections 9' and the caption 'One layer in between: 9 connections.' it says the layered design needs 5 edits, the opposite of the point (1). The lesson app sets this counter to '-' after the abstraction is toggled for exactly this reason.
findings.fix: In the calm layered state show '-' (or hide the 'to edit' stat) until the second change starts at 9.75 s, then count 5 -> 1. In update(): `const calm = ...; text: calm ? '-' : nEdit` (or k: 0 while calm).
findings.evidence: ds-1 s10@8.4 (connections 9, to edit 5 in grey); lesson ds-04.js: `qs('#ce', card).textContent = '-'` in the toggle handler.

findings.problem: Caption 4 'Even repairs take it offline.' (and the grey 'maintenance: repairs need downtime' tag) is not shown by the picture: the wrench lands on a server that is already dead and red from the crash (5.8 s), so it reads as 'we fix the crash', not as 'even a planned repair needs the system to go down' (the lesson's third limitation: hard to update or fix without downtime).
findings.fix: Show a healthy server for the third beat: revive the server to green at about 7.3 s, then the wrench arrives and the server goes grey/'down' because of the repair (stream stops), with the caption 'Even a repair means downtime.' Or change the caption to what is actually drawn only if the planned-repair idea is dropped.
findings.evidence: ds-1 s2@8.6 (dead server with a wrench, served 0 / dropped 9,000).

findings.problem: The lecture's key distinction is never written on screen. 'fault' is only a tag on one orange dot and 'failures: N' a counter; nothing says fault = one part misbehaves and failure = the service stops for users. The title and captions use both words before either is defined, so a first-time learner cannot tell why the same dead disk is 'a fault' at 4 s and 'a failure' at 6 s.
findings.fix: Add two small legend tags, e.g. orange 'fault: one part breaks' (with the first 'fault' tag, 2.9 s) and red 'failure: users lose the service' (when row 1 pops, 4.6 s), or give the 'failures' tag that wording. Keep captions as they are.
findings.evidence: ds-1 s5@2.5, s5@5.5, s5@6.6 (no definition of fault or failure anywhere on screen).

findings.problem: The lesson's contrast between HARDWARE faults (mostly independent: one server dies, the others share its load) and SOFTWARE faults (correlated: the same bug on every node) is carried only by a bolt icon and a bug icon; the words 'hardware' and 'software' appear only in the code comments. Captions say 'One dies' and 'One bug hits all six together', so the learner is not told why six servers did not help against the bug, which is the reason for the whole beat.
findings.fix: Add a small tag 'hardware fault: independent' by the first two bolts (2.3 s) and 'software bug: same code on all six' with the bug (9.85 s); optionally caption 5 'One bug, same code on all six: all fail together.' (length is ok at about 17 characters a second if the window is widened).
findings.evidence: ds-1 s6@2.3 (bolt, no label), s6@10.2 (bug, no label); lesson ds-reliability steps 'Hardware faults happen constantly' / 'Software faults are sneakier' and L['ds-reliability'].guide.

findings.problem: The 'served' and 'dropped' stats show bare numbers (6,000, 3,000, 9,000) although they are per-second rates (the server says '9,000/s'); after the users stop sending (about 7 s) the rail is empty but the stats still hold 'served 0 / dropped 9,000', which can be read as a cumulative total. Also at 5.9 s caption 3 'everything is down' starts while the counters are still falling (served 5,100).
findings.fix: Write the stat values as '6,000/s' and '3,000/s' (or label them 'served per second' / 'dropped per second').

findings.problem: The two answers are shown one after the other for the same customer: first New York refuses (cross, 'no answer'), then at 8.9 s it answers '5'. Nothing says these are two alternative worlds ('either ... or'), so it can read as 'New York refused, then answered anyway'.
findings.fix: Add an 'or' tag between the two answer cards, or caption 5 'Or stay available: answer, maybe stale.', and/or clear the cross and reset the customer to grey before the second run.
findings.evidence: ds-1 s3@7.6 (cross, 'no answer'), s3@9.3 (cross gone, red 5 arrives at the same customer).

findings.problem: (1) The title says 'behind every data app'; the lesson says 'almost every data app'. (2) 'no index: ... 1,000,000 checks' is the WORST case (the lesson labels it 'Worst-case checks'; the average full scan is about half that) and the index bar's '20 checks' is 'about 20' (log2 of a million = 19.9); the 'with an index' sliver is also far wider than 20 / 1,000,000 of the bar (visual only). (3) Caption 2 'A cache keeps answers close: 2 ms, not 100.' starts at 4.4 s but the '100 ms' tag appears at 5.35 s and the '2 ms' tag at 6.35 s, so the numbers are read about one second before they are on screen.
findings.fix: (1) 'Four building blocks behind most data apps'. (2) Label the red bar 'up to 1,000,000 checks' and the green one 'about 20 checks'. (3) Move caption 2's start to about 5.4 s, or split it ('A cache keeps answers close.' / '2 ms, not 100.').
findings.evidence: ds-1 s4@8.9 (bars), s4@4.7 and s4@5.7 (caption 2 on screen, no ms tags yet); lesson ds-blocks (ix demo 'Worst-case checks', 'about 20').

findings.problem: The seven orange markers stay on the field for the whole week, so day 7 looks like seven dead disks at once, but the lesson's model replaces a dead disk after 3 days (D1.DISKS.replace = 3 is simulated but never shown or said). The 'disk faults 7' counter is right as a weekly total; the field reads as 'currently dead' and 'failures: 7' as seven simultaneous outages.
findings.fix: Say it on the field: 'faults this week' under the counter, or fade a marker 3 days after it appears (and keep the 7 total); or tag the field 'dead disks over 7 days'.
findings.evidence: ds-1 s5@5.5 (day 7, seven markers); videos/d1/common.js DISKS.replace = 3.

findings.problem: The 'reads' counter in phase A counts LOOKUPS (3 for Ana in approach 1), while the bar and caption 5 use 'timeline reads per second' / 'reads' for whole timeline views (300,000, '65 reads per post'). Same word, two meanings (the lesson does the same, but a first-time viewer sees 'reads 3' for one timeline).
findings.fix: Relabel the phase A counter 'lookups' (matching caption 2 'Reading means 3 lookups and a merge.') and keep 'reads' for the 300,000 bar.
findings.evidence: ds-1 s8@4.9 (reads 3 for one timeline) vs s8@9.9 ('timeline reads per second').

findings.problem: All five captions run at 17.6 to 18.0 characters per second (house rule: about 17 or slower), the fastest of the video.
findings.fix: Shorten or lengthen the windows by about 0.1 s each (for example 'Three kinds of easy: run, understand, change.' 0.75-3.4 s; 'One layer in between: 9 connections.' 8.35-10.45 s).

findings.problem: The recap's third row says 'Easy to run, understand, change' but its pictogram (apps, layer, six tangled links becoming five tidy ones) only shows abstraction (simplicity and evolvability), nothing about running; and the three rows leave out the lecture's first trade-off (consistent or available, lesson takeaway 'two trade-offs') and the percentile idea. Both choices follow the three-row template, but the row-2 label 'Add machines as load grows' also drops the 'scale up or out' choice.
findings.fix: Optional: relabel row 3 'Hide the mess behind a layer' (or keep the label and add a small gear/wrench to the pictogram) and, if there is room in the label, change row 2 to 'Scale out, don't just scale up'. No number changes needed (6 vs 5 links, 3,000 of 9,000 dropped, 75% left are all correct).
